title: What is the cheapest payment-and-audit protocol that makes honest ML training an equilibrium?
lede: research programme: incentive-compatible verification of outsourced ML training; first measurement on real training finds a tolerance-tau referee passes a skip-steps cheat on 30% of steps at tau = 1e-2 while the held-out loss stays within one seed std, and the loss only suffers at tau about 10x the worst benign drift; milestone 4 prices contracts by linear programme: with a tolerance, audit-only cannot enforce full effort and the joint contract beats both checks only when the score is precise (4 of 45 cells); milestone 6: against a coordinating majority replication adds no deterrence beyond the audit and the stake is flat in the number of workers (140 cells); milestone 5: an agreement term between redundant workers is worth nothing beyond the audit once cheats copy one trajectory (0 of 1,349 random instances), and a proved one-sided bound max(C, g/p - S) holds in 2,755 instances but is vacuous for a noisy score
summary: An open research programme rather than a finished project. A requester pays untrusted workers to train a model; cheating is cheap and the product cannot be checked without redoing the work. The programme asks for the cheapest protocol that makes full-effort training an equilibrium when the checks are a refereed re-execution of a disputed step, a noisy proper score of the final model on held-out data, and agreement among redundant workers, and when honest workers disagree by floating-point drift. It consolidates about 60 stylised projects in this repository (verification-game, audit-allocation, verifier-bribery, effort-elicitation, reproducible-refereed-training and others). Planned: the drift tolerance priced as a cheating margin, a joint contract over audit rate, stake and score with a proved cost frontier, the stake needed against workers who share one cheap trajectory, and measurement on real small-model training. First result (H1, milestone 3): on a 64-64-10 MLP trained on the real scikit-learn digits data over 20 seeds, a referee that accepts a step within L2 distance tau passes a worker that skips, subsamples or lowers precision whenever the alternative is within tau. Benign float16 drift is at most 9×10−3 (median 3×10−5); skipping passes 30% of steps at tau = 10−2 and costs less than one seed standard deviation of held-out loss, and costs 30 standard deviations only at tau = 0.1. At drift-sized tolerances the margin is saved work rather than a worse model. One dataset, one small model and plain SGD; Milestone 4 (H2, first look) solves the cheapest contract as a linear programme on the measured skip actions: once the tolerance exceeds benign drift, audit-only cannot implement full effort at any stake, score-only costs 5.8 compute units at 540 test examples, and the joint contract is strictly cheaper than the better single check in 4 of 45 settings (ratios 0.72 to 0.81, all with 5,000 test examples). A requester who buys the quality the tolerance sanctions instead pays the effort plus one audited step. One model, the skip family only, a Gaussian score; Milestone 5 (H3, H5): with two redundant workers an agreement term lowers the cheapest contract only when cheats cannot coordinate; with one shared cheap trajectory and copying equilibria excluded it never beat the audit in 1,349 random linear-programme instances (the parameters are swept, not measured). A one-sided resolution lower bound max(C, g/p − S) is proved and never violated, exact in 2,410 of 2,755 random instances, but the proposal's constant-factor claim fails (worst ratio 2,093) and the bound is vacuous for a Gaussian score. Milestone 6 (H4): brute-force search over strong equilibria with m = 1 to 7 replicated workers sharing one cheap trajectory finds that a coalition of floor(m/2)+1 escapes replication, and that the stake deterring it, max(0, g/p − 1), does not fall with m (matches in all 140 cells), so the proposal's 1/m law is refuted for a per-job audit; the result is a model check (pure strategies, one shared cheat). H6 is untested. Milestone 34 (H4): with the auditor as a player, a catch reward cannot deter it (it earns 0 in the honest profile), and the bond that does grows about linearly in the number of workers (17 at m = 1, 134 at m = 7; brute force matches the closed form in 440 instances).
